title: Sim2Real VLA: Zero-Shot Generalization of Synthesized Skills to Realistic Manipulation
one_liner: A robot model trained only on fake data learns to work in the real world by splitting the job into two simpler pieces: a high-level planner that finds the right sequence of moves, and a low-level actor that makes those moves actually happen.
lead: Training robots on simulated data is cheap and safe, but when a real robot tries to copy what it learned, things often go wrong. Sim2Real VLA solves this by splitting the problem: a high-level planner figures out which way to reach for an object (the chain of steps), and a low-level actor makes those steps real in the actual world. The trick is that each piece filters out the stuff that does not matter and focuses only on what the robot's body actually needs to do.

problem.h2: Simulators are fast, but the real world is messy
paras: A robot trained in a perfect virtual world has a problem: the real world is sloppy. Lighting changes. Materials feel different. Surfaces shift. A policy (the robot's decision-making rules) that worked in simulation often just freezes up or flails when it first touches a real object.

A naive solution is to collect real robot videos and retrain. But real data is slow, expensive, and risky — robots break things, take time, need experts to supervise. That is why everyone wants a model that trains on fake data and transfers without retraining.

callout.html: A robot policy trained on clean simulated images and actions fails in the real world because the visual details and physics are just too different.

panels.title: 1. Training in a fake world
panels.caption: Robot learns from perfect simulator with clean pixels and exact physics.

panels.title: 2. Reality shocks the trained policy
panels.caption: Real images are messy. Policy sees unexpected textures, shadows, reflections it never trained on.

panels.title: 3. Split the job into two brains
panels.viz_args: High-level planner asks: reach left or right? Low-level actor says: move arm this fast.
panels.caption: Planner ignores visual clutter, focuses on object location. Actor ignores everything but motion.

panels.title: 4. Each piece ignores the noise it does not need
panels.caption: Planner sees only object center. Actor sees only force and speed. Each filters its own junk.

panels.title: 5. Zero-shot transfer works
panels.caption: Robot trained on fake data succeeds on real object it has never seen before.

steps.text: High-level model looks at the object and predicts the sequence of reachable positions and grasp angles to get to the goal.

steps.b: Planner outputs a chain of steps
steps.text: Instead of raw coordinates, it outputs a symbolic sequence: reach-left, rotate-wrist, lower-fingers, etc.
Low-level model takes one affordance step and outputs actual motor commands: joint angles, forces, velocities.
Feedback sensors (cameras, force gauges, joint encoders) tell the actor if the plan is working or needs correction.

Planner trained on fake object images still recognizes real objects because affordances are about object shape, not texture. Actor trained on fake physics still works because motor commands are about the robot body, not world pixels.

object.h2: What the paper changes: two independent heads instead of one
paras: Most VLA models (Vision-Language-Action — a model that looks at images, understands text goals, and outputs robot actions) have one decoder that reads the image and directly predicts the action. This all-in-one head has to solve two contradictory problems at once: ignore the visual noise while still following the actual object motion, and predict abstract affordances while also saying exactly which joint to move. Sim2Real VLA splits this into two independent prediction heads: a planner that ignores motor details and an actor that ignores visual clutter, each handling a simpler task.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: which visual details actually matter for the real world
hidden.name: affordance-relevance signal
paras: Every pixel in a real image carries noise the robot does not need: a shadow that shifts, a reflection, a texture that looks different from the simulator. But some details matter: the angle and position of the object it is trying to grasp. The paper does not explicitly measure this signal, but the architecture implicitly discovers it: the planner learns to extract only shape-based affordances (reachable positions, grasp angles, motion sequences) from images, throwing away lighting, material, and surface detail. The actor, in turn, learns what the robot body actually felt during training and ignores visual input entirely when executing.

By routing planner outputs through a tokenized action space (a small, discrete vocabulary of named affordances like grab-center, slide-left, lift, rotate), the paper forces the split: the token becomes the bottleneck that lets only task-relevant information pass from planner to actor.

heat.caption: Darker means more critical for real-world success. Object shape and motion matter. Visual noise does not.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the set of details in a real-world image that actually affect whether the robot succeeds or fails. Sim2Real VLA implicitly learns this by making the planner ignore pixels it does not need (textures, shadows) and the actor ignore pixels it does not see (it focuses on force and position feedback instead).

The paper calls this the affordance decomposition: it identifies which scene features map to which action primitives. The tokenized action space is the mechanism: a small discrete vocabulary of reachable affordances acts as a lossy gate, passing high-level task structure while dropping visual minutiae.

mechanism.h2: Why two heads work better than one
paras: When one model has to solve two different prediction tasks at once, the neural network ends up learning a compromise: features that help with visual understanding (like which pixels contain edges and textures) interfere with motor prediction, because the network is forced to compress both jobs into one learned representation. The planner has to deal with grasp angles and reachability, which are about object shape but also visual. The actor has to deal with motor commands and forces, which are physical but not visual at all. By forcing a bottleneck — the tokenized affordance space — the paper makes each head specialize. The planner learns the semantic structure of the task (what moves are feasible given the object), and the actor learns the kinematic structure of the robot body (which joints to move to perform each affordance). The act of splitting not only makes each head simpler, it also lets each one survive the domain shift: a planner trained on fake 3D shapes still recognizes real shapes because shape is shape. An actor trained on fake robot dynamics still works on a real robot because inertia is inertia. The mismatch between fake and real pixels no longer breaks the pipeline because the planner-to-actor handoff is not pixels, it is the high-level semantic affordance — which does not change between simulation and reality.

math.h2: One simple loss: weighted sum of two separate predictions
math.words: total loss equals (planner prediction error) plus lambda times (actor prediction error). Planner is penalized only on affordance accuracy. Actor is penalized only on action accuracy.
symbols: error of planner on predicting the affordance chain
error of actor on predicting motor commands given affordances
weight that trades off planner and actor performance during training

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the planner predicts the wrong affordance chain and loses 0.8 points. The actor predicts the motor commands correctly given that chain and loses 0.2 points.
Now suppose we increase lambda to 2.0 because we care more about executing affordances smoothly.
Total L = 0.8 + 2.0 * 0.2 = 1.2 — the actor error is now weighted twice as heavy, so training will push the actor to be more careful.

If the planner had mispredicted with L_planner = 2.0, total would be 2.0 + 2.0 * 0.2 = 2.4, so the planner error dominates. Adjusting lambda tunes the tradeoff between high-level and low-level accuracy.

math.note: The loss splits the problem: the planner learns to output a valid affordance chain, the actor learns to translate affordances to robot motion. Each piece optimizes its own error independently.

bars.h2: How the two-head approach beats the naive one-head baseline

charts.title: One-head VLA (trained on sim, tested on real)
charts.note: Single decoder tries to be visual and motor at once. Real images confuse it. Fails unpredictably.

charts.title: Sim2Real VLA (two heads, trained on sim only)
charts.note: Planner and actor each solve a simpler problem. Specialization lets affordances survive the domain gap. Numbers are illustrative; this is a teaching example.

items.b: Planner predicts an impossible affordance chain.
items.html: If the planner has never seen a certain object configuration in simulation, it might output an affordance that is not physically reachable on the real robot. The actor will try to execute it, fail, and the whole task falls apart. This fails silently: the robot does not say I cannot reach that, it just does not reach it.

items.b: Actor learns fake robot physics, not real physics.
items.html: If the simulator gets friction, inertia, or cable compliance wrong, the actor will predict motor commands that do not account for real-world spring-back or stiction. Small errors in the simulator compound: over many steps, the robot drifts off target.

items.b: Tokenized affordance space is too coarse.
items.html: If the vocabulary of named affordances is too small, the planner cannot express fine-grained differences: should I reach at 45 degrees or 50 degrees? A bucket labeled reach is not fine enough. The actor then has to improvise, and improvisation in a real robot is dangerous.

Pair the two-head model with a human or automated safety checker that watches the actor's output before it reaches the motors. If the affordance chain looks wrong or the motor commands are suspiciously large, reject the action and ask for a retry. This adds latency but prevents silent failures.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small simulator with a single gripper arm and three object shapes (a cube, a cylinder, a ball). Generate 500 synthetic training trajectories: reach, grasp, lift, place. Train Sim2Real VLA (planner + actor) on the synthetic data. Test on real objects the model has never seen (different sizes, different textures, placed in new locations). Measure success: did the arm lift the object into the target zone? Run the same task on a one-head baseline VLA baseline trained on the same synthetic data. Compare how often each model succeeds when the object textures and materials are changed between training and test.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (number of tasks where robot lifted object) / (total tasks attempted)
demo.closing: The demo will show that the two-head approach (Sim2Real VLA) succeeds far more often than the one-head baseline when facing real-world variability, because the planner ignores visual noise and the actor ignores pixels, allowing each to specialize.
